title: Why the Radium Girls Licked Poison
topic: Why the radium girls licked their paintbrushes

lines: A young woman licks the tip of her paintbrush at work.
Then she dips it in glowing paint and paints a watch dial.
She does this all day, every day.
Her name is Grace Fryer. She paints watch faces for the army.
Her boss tells her the paint is safe.
She earns about a penny and a half per dial.
Her teeth start to ache. Then they fall out.
Her jaw breaks. Her bones snap.
Doctors see women with loose teeth and ulcers that won't heal.
The company says the women are showing signs of infection.
They tell the women radium is safe.
You see, it's like when you're told not to touch something hot.
But everyone around you says it's fine.
So you touch it. Again and again.
The real reason is the paint.
It's made from powdered radium, a radioactive metal.
Radium shoots out tiny particles that break your bones from inside.
The women swallowed it with every lick.
The man who invented the paint died from it too.
Radium was sold as a health cure for years.
The same poison that killed them was advertised as medicine.

claims.claim: Supervisors encouraged workers to shape brushes with their lips ("lip, dip, paint") to save time and material.
Grace Fryer was a plant worker who decided to sue, but it took two years to find a lawyer willing to take on USRC.
Workers were paid about a penny and a half per dial, earning $3.75 for 250 dials per shift.
Women developed dental pain, loose teeth, lesions, ulcers, anemia, bone fractures, and necrosis of the jaw (radium jaw).
When word of the New Jersey suits appeared in newspapers, women were told the radium was safe and that New Jersey employees were showing signs of viral infections.
The paint was made from powdered radium, zinc sulfide, gum arabic, and water.
Radium emits gamma rays that can penetrate a glass watch dial and into human tissue.
Dr. Sabin Arnold von Sochocky invented radium dial paint and died in November 1928 from radiation exposure.
Radium was advertised as a cure-all and used in cosmetic products promising regenerative anti-aging properties.
